title: Cyclists killed or seriously injured
description: A cyclist was killed or seriously injured ("incapacitating" in police records) in 217 crashes in the 12 months through 2026-07-26, vs 169 the prior 12 months. Vision Zero's goal is zero.
caveat: Police-reported crashes in which a cyclist was killed or seriously injured, counted over the 12 months ending 2026-07-26 (217 crashes). The most recent 2 months are provisional — police records are amended for weeks after a crash, so this figure can rise. Counts are not adjusted for how many people ride, so growth in cycling is not netted out.

title: How much of the network protects riders
description: Only 15% of Chicago's 446 on-street bikeway miles are physically protected lanes (69 mi); counting buffered lanes brings it to 39%. The rest is paint, sharrows, and greenways. Off-street trails are tracked separately.
caveat: Share of current on-street network mileage as of 2026-07-27; protected = barrier/curb-protected on-street lanes. Off-street trails are excluded — they live in the separate OSM layer.

title: How much of the street grid has bike infrastructure
description: Chicago has 3,944 miles of surface streets (arterials, collectors, and neighborhood streets). 446 miles — 11% — have any bike infrastructure at all, counting everything from sharrows to protected lanes.
caveat: Centerline miles on both sides of the ratio. Expressways, ramps, alleys, and river channels are excluded from street miles; off-street trails are excluded from bikeway miles. The street centerline layer was last updated in 2021 — the grid changes slowly.

title: Highest crash-density corridors
description: Top corridors by cyclist crashes per km of bikeway: Kinzie (79.67/km); Wells (51.67/km); Clark (46.48/km); Milwaukee (43.2/km); Dearborn (37.44/km).
caveat: Cyclist crashes reported from September 2017 through 2026-07-26, divided by each corridor's bikeway kilometres. Not adjusted for how many people ride, so a busier corridor can rank higher without being more dangerous per rider. Dooring is undercounted in police records, so every corridor's count here is a floor. The shortest corridors — Kinzie among them — compute their rate over very few kilometres, which makes those rates unstable rather than a finding.

title: How often the driver leaves
description: In 27% of police-reported cyclist crashes since Sept 2017 (4692 of 17432), the driver left the scene — 27% when the cyclist was injured.
caveat: Share of police-reported cyclist crashes reported from September 2017 through 2026-07-26 in which the driver left the scene. Crashes that were never reported to police are on neither side of this share, so it describes reported crashes only and the true rate is unknown.

title: Ward concentration
description: 5 of 50 wards account for 27% of located cyclist crashes since Sept 2017: Ward 27 (1200), Ward 42 (1112), Ward 32 (825), Ward 1 (822), Ward 34 (663).
caveat: Located cyclist crashes reported from September 2017 through 2026-07-26, summed by ward — the five highest-count wards against all 50. Ward totals are not adjusted for how many people ride, so a ward with heavy bike traffic can top this list without having the most dangerous streets.

title: Dooring: structurally undercounted
description: 2050 crashes since Sept 2017 carry a dooring flag. Dooring is structurally excluded from 'reportable' crash records unless damage/injury thresholds are met, so the real number is higher than any count on this site.
caveat: Cyclist crashes reported from September 2017 through 2026-07-26 that carry a dooring flag in the police record (2050 crashes). Dooring is excluded from reportable crash records unless a damage or injury threshold is met, so this is a floor on dooring crashes and not a full count.

title: How Chicago's bike network scores nationally
description: PeopleForBikes' Bicycle Network Analysis scores how much of Chicago a person can reach on low-stress streets — and gives the city 11.08 out of 100. The average rated U.S. city scores 36. Among the 73 rated U.S. cities over 300,000 people, Chicago ranks last. Behind the number: 6,267 miles of high-stress streets versus 1,834 low-stress. That's up slightly from 9 in 2024. This grades the network, not crashes: it can move independently of any crash trend, because it measures what's built, not what happened.
caveat: Third-party score, analysis 26.05 (May 2026). Computed by PeopleForBikes from OpenStreetMap — only as current as volunteer mapping, which is uneven across neighborhoods; it can understate what a neighborhood has, or miss hazards nobody mapped. PFB's scoring methodology has changed over the years (notably 2020 and 2026), so history entries are not comparable across distant analysis versions. It grades the street network, not the people riding it — a low score is a case for building more, not a reason not to ride.

title: Promised bikeway miles vs. what got built
description: CDOT's 2023 Chicago Cycling Strategy commits to 150 miles of new bikeways, 80% of them low-stress. Using CDOT's own year-by-year installation figures (2023–2025), the city has built 103.8 miles of genuinely new bikeway — 69% of the pledge. CDOT itself reports 125.9 miles (84%) toward the same goal, but 22.0 of those miles are concrete upgrades to protected lanes that already existed, not new bikeway. On the low-stress pledge, 80.3% of the miles CDOT counts are low-stress; counting only genuinely new miles, 76.2%. Source: Chicago Department of Transportation, 2023 Chicago Cycling Strategy; installation figures from CDOT FOIA S145367-071326, released 2026-07-24.
caveat: Both figures cover 2023–2025 and come from CDOT's own Complete Streets dashboard, so the gap is a counting difference, not a dispute about the underlying miles. The pledge says "new bikeways," which is why the headline excludes the 22.0 miles of concrete upgrades; CDOT's larger number is shown alongside so both countings are visible. Low-stress here means protected lanes, neighborhood greenways, and off-street trails — buffered and painted lanes and sharrows are excluded, the same way this site's network map grades them, and the same way CDOT's own dashboard counts them. The pledge carries no published deadline, so this is progress through 2025, not a verdict on whether CDOT will meet it.
